title: Arjuna becomes a student
hookLine: the greatest archer drops his bow and says: i'm your student. teach me
carry: bow, ask, serve: how Hindus learn from a guru

cards: A first meeting with someone who knows far more than you: a new boss, a professor, a friend's grandmother. Two easy mistakes: act like you know it all, or nod in silence, too polite to ask.

Now picture the greatest archer alive, Arjuna, on a battlefield, his bow fallen beside him, too torn to fight his own family. He turns to his charioteer, Krishna, and says: I'm your student. I come to you for refuge.

teach.b: That one sentence starts the whole Bhagavad Gita, and later Krishna tells him how a student learns from the wise. Learn it by bowing down, by asking, by serving. The wise, who have seen the truth, will teach you.
Pranipata: bowing down, a body bent toward the person.
Pariprashna: asking, all the way around a thing. Seva: service, being useful to the one who teaches. Look at the middle word.

This isn't silent awe. And Arjuna lives it: for the rest of the Gita he keeps asking, hard, and Krishna keeps answering. Here's the teaching: the bond of guru and student, one of the oldest things in Hinduism.
Respect makes room for the questions instead of shutting them down.
The Mundaka Upanishad adds one detail: the seeker goes to a teacher fuel in hand, carrying firewood for the teacher's fire. You arrive bringing something useful, not just a need.
So the graduate's path doesn't end the learning. It changes the classroom: bowed, curious, and carrying a little wood.

how: In some Hindu settings a student greets a teacher by bowing or touching the teacher's feet, asks questions after the lesson, and helps with the teacher's work; Gita 4.34 is often quoted for this.

games.q: you get one hour with a scholar you admire. by the Gita's verse, how do you spend it?
o: show what you know, so they'll take you seriously.
bow, ask your real questions, offer to help.
listen in silence; questions would be rude.
games.why: bowing down, asking, serving: Gita 4.34. the respect makes room for the questions; the wise who have seen the truth will teach.

practice: Join your palms at your chest and bow your head a little: the pranam offered to a teacher or an elder. Notice how the breath changes.
Then lift your head as if about to ask a question, and stay there, open and curious, for the rest of the sit. If you don't pray, let the bow be to anyone who has taught you.

wordCard.voice: The graduate's path: after study, finding the wise again, and meeting them the Gita's way, bowing, asking, serving.

orig.note: Sanskrit: asking all around, thorough questioning; the middle move of Gita 4.34.

carryVoice: Your line: bow, ask, serve: how Hindus learn from a guru. Come with some wood. That's today.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.47 and 2.7 (Arjuna sets down his bow; 'I am your disciple; teach me, who have taken refuge in you')
Bhagavad Gita 4.34 (learn it by prostration, by inquiry, by service; the wise who have seen the truth will teach you knowledge)
Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.12 (to know it, let him go, fuel in hand, to a teacher learned and established in Brahman)
